name: Classic
summary: Familiar and always there: a left-aligned taskbar with Start, apps, tray and clock, full title bars and your desktop icons.
description: A familiar desktop: a full-width taskbar along the bottom with Start, search and apps on the left and Quick Settings, notifications and the clock on the right; minimize and maximize buttons on every window; desktop icons kept. No hot corner, so nothing happens by surprise.

settings.reason: Original JERONIX icons; anything JERONIX does not draw falls back to Adwaita.
Neutral, quiet system sounds.
Older (GTK 3) applications use a neutral dark theme with a blue accent.
A neutral, highly legible interface typeface.
Documents use the same neutral typeface.
JERONIX's primary dark look.
Blue is the JERONIX accent: buttons, switches and selections in every app.
A neutral monospace typeface for the terminal and code.
The neutral pointer.
Nothing opens unless you ask for it.
Weekday next to the time.
Familiar title bar buttons.
Double-click a title bar to maximize, as on most desktops.
Workspaces appear as needed.
New windows open in the middle of the screen.
JERONIX light wallpaper.
JERONIX dark wallpaper.
Fill the screen without distortion.
The JERONIX menu is labeled, like a start menu.
Workspaces are always visible in the top bar.
The focused application and its windows menu are always visible.
The JERONIX menu replaces Activities.
A taskbar along the bottom edge, like most desktops.
Always visible; windows maximize next to it, never under it.
Compact taskbar icons.
Running applications appear after favorites.
Window previews on hover.
A full-width taskbar.
Start and apps aligned left, like a classic taskbar.
Quick Settings and the clock with notifications live in the taskbar tray.
One bar: GNOME's top bar is hidden while the taskbar carries the tray.
Task View opens the windows and workspaces overview.
A Start button at the head of the taskbar.
Search finds apps, files and settings from the taskbar.
The Super key opens Start, as the Windows key does.
Task View shows windows and workspaces only; apps live in Start.
The free end of the taskbar shows what is going on and opens the widgets.

limitations: Window snapping is left to the system: GNOME's edge tiling, or Ubuntu's Tiling Assistant where it is installed (it turns GNOME's off while it runs).
Desktop icons (ding) are left as they are.
The dock lives on the primary monitor only.
